content: The comparison of treatment regimens for multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) that include bedaquiline versus those that do not, as per WHO guidelines, has been limited by the lack of direct head-to-head trials. Current evidence suggests that dosage guidance for MDR-TB medications is unlikely to change based on findings from systematic reviews due to the limited comparative data available. For children under three years of age with MDR/RR-TB, the use of all-oral treatment regimens containing delamanid, compared to regimens without delamanid, remains a topic of interest. All patients diagnosed with rifampicin-resistant TB (RR-TB) are eligible for MDR/RR-TB treatment regimens, which should include effective medications of good quality, management of adverse events, and patient support. Longer treatment regimens with sufficient effective agents have been shown to improve cure rates and reduce mortality in both adults and children. These regimens are typically individualized to the patient’s needs and last 18–20 months or longer, with adjustments based on the patient’s response to therapy. In 2018, WHO recommended a total treatment duration of 18–20 months, with 15–17 months of treatment following culture conversion for most patients. These recommendations were based on individual patient data (IPD) meta-analyses, which heavily relied on observational studies rather than randomized controlled trials (RCTs). As a result, the certainty of evidence was often graded as low or very low. The 2018 IPD meta-analysis included data from 13,104 patients across 53 studies in 40 countries. This analysis provided insights into treatment success, failure, relapse, and death associated with individual medicines in longer MDR/RR-TB regimens. However, the evidence for the effectiveness of many medications used in these regimens remains limited, with few studies employing randomized designs. For children under six years of age, the use of bedaquiline in MDR/RR-TB treatment was evaluated using data from two Phase 2 trials (TMC207-C211 and IMPAACT P1108). Although the sample size was small, the data suggested that cardiac safety signals in children were not distinct from those observed in adults. The 2018 WHO guidelines categorized MDR-TB medications into three groups based on their effectiveness and safety profiles. Group A (highly effective agents) includes fluoroquinolones, bedaquiline, and linezolid, which are strongly recommended unless contraindicated. Group B (conditionally recommended agents) includes clofazimine and cycloserine/terizidone. Group C includes other medications used when regimens cannot be composed with Group A or B agents. Kanamycin and capreomycin are no longer recommended due to poor outcomes, and gatifloxacin and high-dose isoniazid are rarely used due to limited availability and safety concerns. The concurrent use of bedaquiline and delamanid has been studied in limited patient cohorts, with data suggesting potential benefits but insufficient evidence to make strong recommendations. Safety data from the DELIBERATE trial and other studies have informed the use of these drugs, particularly in vulnerable populations such as pregnant women and children. For children under six years of age, the benefits of using bedaquiline likely outweigh the risks, though more data are needed to strengthen these recommendations. The development of child-friendly formulations, such as a 20 mg scored uncoated tablet of bedaquiline, is expected to improve treatment options for younger children.
